week.summary: The evidence leans modestly bearish. Three briefings, all issued 17 to 19 November, reached the same verdict at strength -1. Confirmed inventory data drove the view: a 3.38 million barrel US crude build and a 5.19 million barrel gasoline build in the EIA report, preceded by a 5.28 million barrel API build. The IEA's Q4 2026 surplus estimate of 1.7 million bpd, a hawkish Fed with the dollar at a 19-month high, and recovering Gulf and OPEC output add to the surplus case. Against this, Hormuz and Red Sea attacks continue, Hormuz throughput was cited at only about 49% of pre-war levels, and speculative length sits near the 12th percentile of three years. Brent moved from 91.70 to 89.82 dollars a barrel (-2.1%), and the two scored calls produced one hit and one miss. The sample is small and the day-by-day verdicts are weak, so confidence is low.

bullish_drivers.driver: Confirmed attacks on Hormuz shipping, including the ADNOC L&S vessel hit with one crew member missing and 11 injured, plus US strikes on Qeshm and Iranian and Houthi launches at Gulf states. The further Iranian mine claims on 19 November are unconfirmed and carry little weight.
Houthi gains around Bab el-Mandeb and Aden, and missiles reaching Riyadh. The 17 and 18 November items were confirmed; the PIF Tower damage on 19 November is only reported.

Physical tightness and light positioning. The Brent January-February backwardation widened from $2.45 to $2.64 to $2.81 over the period. Managed money was at the 11.6th percentile of three years, which leaves room for short-covering.
Fragile Hormuz recovery, with throughput about 49% of pre-war levels according to ANZ, and analyst warnings (TD Securities, BMI) that a risk premium should be rebuilt.

bearish_drivers.driver: Confirmed US stock builds: API crude +5.28 million barrels, then EIA crude +3.38 million and gasoline +5.19 million, with a shut WTI export arbitrage adding pressure.
IEA November report: Q4 2026 supply 1.7 million bpd above demand and a 2027 surplus of 3.8 million bpd. Goldman expects Brent to average $88 in 2027.
Hawkish FOMC minutes (nearly all officials saw further rises as likely appropriate) lifted the dollar to a 19-month high.
Gulf exports and OPEC output recovering toward pre-war levels. The OPEC item is only reported and low impact.
Iran's two-day Hormuz reopening plan, backed by a regional bloc, and Trump's statement that the US and China share an interest in an open Hormuz.

week.narrative_shift: On 17 November the debate was surplus expectations against a cluster of Hormuz attacks, with the IEA report as the anchor. On 18 November the focus moved to the weekly stock data, with the market again selling on inventories despite a confirmed ADNOC attack. By 19 November the EIA build had been confirmed and the macro backdrop turned hawkish. The conflict also widened from shipping lanes to direct strikes on Gulf states. The Shenzhen talks became the main swing factor. Two themes persisted: the market sells attack headlines when stock data are bearish, and light positioning with a steep backwardation keeps upside gap risk alive.
week.price_vs_evidence: Prices were broadly consistent with the bearish evidence over the window, with Brent down 2.1% net. The path was uneven. Brent fell 3.28% into 18 November, a hit, then rose 1.27% on 19 November, a miss. The 18 November briefing says the fall was exaggerated by a contract mismatch in the supplied data, so the exact size of the drop is uncertain. The 19 November headline cites about $92 for the front month while the scorecard shows 89.82, so the price series is not fully reliable. Prices have not fallen further partly because the war premium is not fully removed. The widening backwardation while flat price drifts lower shows that physical tightness persists even as the paper market prices a surplus. The 19 November price rise also fits the FinanceFeeds comment that the Iranian mine reports are holding prices steady, not lifting them.
key_risks: A confirmed loss of Gulf export infrastructure or a verified fall in Hormuz or Red Sea flows.
An unexpected outcome from the Shenzhen talks, in either direction.
Short-covering from the 12th percentile positioning, amplified by implied volatility near 50 (OVX).
Confirmation of the unverified Iranian mine claims or further Houthi strikes on Saudi targets.
A reversal in US inventories, or a hawkish Fed surprise that is larger than priced.
week.what_would_change_it: A verified supply loss, or a Brent move toward the $96 bull case from the FinanceFeeds scenario table, would end the bearish lean. A sustained break below $87 to $88 would confirm and strengthen it. The 29 November OPEC ministerial is the next scheduled test.

month.summary: There are no briefings for days 8 to 31, so the monthly view rests on the same three briefings as the weekly view and adds no independent evidence. The only information on the earlier month is the 18 November remark that Brent had fallen about 18% in 30 days, and the 19 November remark that WTI is at its lowest since August. The consensus is modestly bearish, driven by a shift from a war-premium market to a surplus-pricing market: an IEA surplus of 1.7 million bpd in Q4, consecutive US stock builds, recovering Gulf output and a stronger dollar. The escalation in Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and the Gulf states has not been enough to offset these. Brent ended the covered window at 89.82 dollars a barrel, 2.1% below the first briefing, with a 50% hit rate. Confidence is low because the sample is only three days.

bullish_drivers.driver: Persistent confirmed attacks on Hormuz shipping and Gulf states, with throughput reported at about 49% of pre-war levels. Unverified mine claims on 19 November are given little weight.
Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb coast, an advance toward Aden and missile strikes toward Riyadh.
Steepening Brent backwardation ($2.45 to $2.81) and speculative positioning at the 11.6th to 12th percentile of three years, which leaves room for short-covering.
The US SPR is at 276.4 million barrels, its lowest since August 1982, which leaves less buffer. The briefing labelled this neutral, so it is a minor support.

bearish_drivers.driver: IEA surplus (1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, 3.8 million bpd in 2027) and Goldman's call for Brent at $88 in 2027 and $78 by end-2027.
Confirmed US crude and gasoline builds from API and EIA, and a shut WTI arbitrage to Asia and Europe.
Hawkish Fed minutes and a 19-month high for the dollar.
Gulf and OPEC output recovering, a weak Chinese demand signal (lower refinery runs, resumed stockpiling) and compressing product cracks.

month.narrative_shift: No briefings exist before 17 November, so a month-long narrative cannot be reconstructed. Within the covered days the story moved from IEA surplus versus tanker attacks to weekly stock data and then to macro and diplomacy. The 18% fall over 30 days cited on 18 November implies the market was already shedding its war premium before this window began. The persistent themes are that the market sells on supply-side headlines when inventories are bearish, and that physical tightness and light positioning keep the downside from being one-way.
month.price_vs_evidence: The month-scale evidence, as far as it is supplied, points the same way as the price: a large drawdown of about 18% in 30 days and a net 2.1% fall across the three briefings. The stale EIA STEO forecast (Brent about $100 in November and December, set before the sell-off) shows that official forecasts had not caught up with the market's move to a surplus. Prices also diverged from the confirmed conflict news, because the market treated attacks as already priced or as non-disruptive to flows. The widening backwardation shows the physical market is tighter than the flat price suggests. The contract mismatch noted on 18 November and the $92 versus 89.82 discrepancy on 19 November limit the precision of any price-based conclusion.
key_risks: A confirmed disruption to Gulf export infrastructure or Hormuz and Red Sea flows.
A failed or surprising Shenzhen outcome, or a collapse of Iran's reopening plan.
OPEC ministerial decisions on 29 November, including the difficult 2027 output call.
Short-covering from depleted speculative length, with high implied volatility.
A fall in the surplus forecast if Gulf recovery stalls, or a further dollar-driven slide if the Fed tightens by more than 25 basis points.
month.what_would_change_it: A verified supply loss or a Brent move toward $96 would flip the view bullish. A sustained break below $87 to $88, with further stock builds, would deepen the bearish lean. Additional briefings covering earlier days would also raise confidence in either direction.
